Max Common Chord

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Explore two crossing circles and a bar through P that ends on both circles.
How to play: Drag P or Q to change the circles, or A and B to move the bar. Choose Adjust circles or Adjust chord to decide what dragging A and B does; focus a dot and use arrow keys too.
Look for the math

Move the bar through P and watch the number in the status line. Two lengths change, but their product is tied to a point R on the line through P and Q. The picture is a droodle with a maximum hiding inside it: there is nothing to win.

One product, two ways

A, B and Q lie on one circle. Its chords AB and QR cross at P, so the intersecting chords theorem gives AP × PB = PQ × PR. As P and Q are held fixed while the bar moves, AP × PB grows exactly when PR grows. The logic test checks this equality on thousands of bars, not just the one on screen.

Equal tangents on the axis

The line PQ is the radical axis of the two circles: every point X on it has the same power in both circles, so its two tangents At and Bt have equal lengths. Triangle AtXBt is isosceles, and the base angles that meet the circles again are equal. The test verifies equal tangent lengths and perpendicular radii for hundreds of positions of X.

Where the maximum sits

R is the one point of PQ for which the line AtBt goes through P. At that moment PR, and therefore AP × PB, is as large as it can be for the two circles. The test sweeps every bar direction for several pairs of circles: the line-up happens once, and the product there is the maximum. When points nearly coincide the applet keeps its last drawn frame; this port simply blanks the parts that cannot be computed. Hubert Shutrick found further properties and a synthetic solution, but the construction here is Bogomolny's applet.

Try Adjust chord and drag A until the status says the chord is longest, then press Hint to see the equal tangents and the right angles at At and Bt.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
